title: Model diagnostics and comparison
text: This comparison focuses on the trade-offs between direct estimation, area-level SAE, unit-level SAE models, with and without poststratification.

title: Model diagnostics and comparison
section: 1 Estimate smoothing and target population adjustment
text:
1 Estimate smoothing and target population adjustment
The distribution and rank plots compare the spread of MSOA-year estimates across methods, while the maps compare the local pattern of estimated frequent cycling.

Direct estimates retain the most cell-level variation. Model-based estimates are smoother because they borrow strength across areas, years, predictors, or poststratification cells. The area-level model is anchored by the direct estimates, so weak direct evidence can influence the modelled results.
Differences between the estimates from the two unit-level models are more subtle because they use similar models and spatio-temporal structure. Their main difference is the aggregation step: the poststratified model averages predictions over age-sex-car population cells, while the area-summary model substitutes MSOA-level predictor summaries. Poststratification better aligns predictions with the target population composition; area-summary substitution is more approximate and does not itself correct survey selection bias.











Poststratification changes how the predicted population cells are aggregated. By examining the two MSOAs with the largest increase and decrease after adjusting to the Census population shares, we see that the Cardiff MSOA with higher proportions of groups that are more likely to be frequent cyclists (e.g., 16-49 males with no cars) sees an upward poststratified adjustment compared to the other where there are higher proportions of groups with lower probabilities (e.g., 50+ females with access to a car).

title: Model diagnostics and comparison
text:
2 Uncertainty improvement
Interval width shows the precision gained or lost by each method. Direct-estimate widths reflect sampling variance, while model-based approaches produce credible-interval widths that reflect posterior uncertainty after borrowing strength across areas, years, or predictors.

title: Model diagnostics and comparison
text:
3 Area and temporal effect variance
The inverse precision, 1/\tau, gives the variance scale of each scaled random effect. For the BYM2 term, this is the total residual area-effect variance, combining structured and unstructured components. For the RW1 term, it is the variance scale of the temporal effect across the three survey periods. Larger values indicate that the corresponding random effect accounts for more residual variation, while the intervals show uncertainty in that variance.





The BYM2 mixing parameter, \phi, describes how residual area variation is divided between the structured and unstructured components: values closer to one indicate greater reliance on the adjacency-based structure, while values closer to zero indicate greater reliance on independent area effects.

The lower \phi estimated by the area-level model indicates that less residual variation is attributed to similarities between neighbouring MSOAs. This is consistent with sparse direct estimates and uncertain sampling variances providing limited information from which to identify a coherent spatial pattern.
The unit-level model uses individual responses directly and estimates a higher \phi, attributing more residual variation to the structured component. This allows information to be shared between neighbouring MSOAs and leaves much smaller unstructured area effects. The adjacency structure therefore appears more informative for the unit-level model in this scenario.

title: Survey data
text:
1 About the survey
The analysis uses a harmonised dataset of three waves of the National Survey for Wales (NSW): 2020-2021, 2022-2023, and 2024-2025. The NSW is a repeated cross-sectional survey of people in Wales, with annual survey periods covering transport, health, education, public services, housing, internet access, climate change, and the Welsh language.
The raw survey geography and stratification variable is Local Authority. In this guide, each respondent is assigned to a synthetic MSOA within their Local Authority using random allocation. This serves two purposes:

Higher spatial resolution. The synthetic MSOA assignment supports MSOA-level direct estimation, area-level SAE, spatial modelling, and unit-level SAE with poststratification.
Privacy. The assigned MSOA is not the respondent’s true MSOA, so we avoid presenting fine-grained respondent locations.







Note



In the UK, Local Authorities (LAs) are administrative areas responsible for local government, also referred to as unitary authorities in Wales. Middle Layer Super Output Areas (MSOAs) are smaller statistical areas used to report census and other official statistics in England and Wales. Each contains about 2,000–6,000 households and 5,000–15,000 residents, and lies within a single Local Authority.

title: Survey data
text:
2 Preparation steps for small-area estimation

2.1 Target Estimand
The target estimand is the quantity we want to estimate. It defines the outcome, population, geography, time period, and the auxiliary data needed for modelling, such as predictors or population counts, and can be articulated in the following format. Note that the most common outcomes to estimate are means of continuous variables and prevalence—expressed as shares or proportions—within the target population.
In this guide, our target estimand is:






Target estimand





Outcome: Share of adults who cycle for transport several times weekly
Spatial: MSOAs in Wales
Temporal: Over three survey periods 2020-2021, 2022-2023, and 2024-2025






2.2 Estimation Domains
In spatio-temporal SAE, the estimand is evaluated for every combination of area and time period. Each combination forms an area-time cell for which an estimate is required. The estimation domains are the complete set of these cells.
For the estimand defined above, the estimation domains therefore include every MSOA–year combination, including cells with no survey observations.






Note



With R-INLA, each area and time period is assigned a numeric index.




Code
area_frame <- msoa_boundaries |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  distinct(area_id, msoa_name) |>
  arrange(area_id)

area_index <- area_frame |>
  select(area_id) |>
  arrange(area_id) |>
  mutate(area_inla_id = row_number())

time_index <- survey_microdata |>
  distinct(time_id) |>
  arrange(time_id) |>
  mutate(time_inla_id = row_number())

domain_frame <- tidyr::crossing(area_index, time_index) |>
  left_join(area_frame, by = "area_id") |>
  select(area_id, time_id, area_inla_id, time_inla_id, msoa_name)

write_csv(domain_frame, file.path(base_path, "clean", "domain_msoayear.csv"))

Each survey respondent may also require a design weight and other survey design components if available such as strata. Because the survey question was administered to the full sample in some waves and to a subsample in others, the appropriate weight variable in this case varies by wave:

Use SampleAdultWeight in the 2020-2021 and 2024-2025 survey waves where the active travel module was asked to the main sample.
Use SampleTravelWeight in the 2022-2023 survey wave where the active travel module was asked to only a subsample.

The number of usable observations varies substantially by wave, with the 2023 subsample providing the fewest responses. These averages mask variation between MSOAs, so some area-year estimates will be based on very few observations, motivating the small-area estimation approaches introduced in the following sections.
